summary: A null pointer is a pointer value that deliberately refers to no object or function, guaranteed by the C standard to compare unequal to any valid address. It is the language's way of saying 'nothing here': the end of a linked list, a failed allocation, an optional argument that was not supplied. Dereferencing it is undefined behavior and normally ends in a segmentation fault, so careful C code checks for it at every boundary where a pointer can legitimately be absent.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
Every pointer needs a way to say it points at nothing. Without one, a list node at the end of a chain, a lookup that found no match, or a `malloc` that ran out of memory would have to return some real address that might be mistaken for valid data. C reserves one special value for this purpose, the null pointer, and promises it never equals the address of any object or function.

You get a null pointer by converting a null pointer constant to a pointer type. The standard defines a null pointer constant as an integer constant expression with value 0, or such an expression cast to `void *`. The macro `NULL`, defined in `<stddef.h>`, `<stdio.h>`, `<stdlib.h>` and `<string.h>` among others, expands to an implementation-defined null pointer constant such as `0`, `0L` or `((void *)0)`. The null pointer is a language concept, so what bits it has inside the machine is up to the implementation, although nearly all platforms use all-bits-zero.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
bullets: **Null pointer constant**: an integer constant expression with value 0, or that cast to `void *`. Both `0` and `(void *)0` qualify, so `int *p = 0;` is valid.
**`NULL`**: a macro for a null pointer constant, available in several standard headers. Prefer it to a bare `0` because it shows intent.
**Null pointer**: the value you get when a null pointer constant is converted to a pointer type. It compares unequal to every pointer to an object or function.
**Every pointer type has one**: `int *p = NULL;` and `char *q = NULL;` are both fine. Two null pointers of any types compare equal after conversion.
**Truthiness**: a null pointer is false in conditions, and every other pointer is true, so `if (p)` and `if (p != NULL)` mean the same.
**Dereferencing is undefined**: `*p` for null `p` has no defined behavior. On typical systems the lowest page of virtual memory is unmapped so it traps with `SIGSEGV`.
**Null versus zero value**: a null pointer is not the number 0 in memory as far as the language is concerned, only the constant 0 in pointer context converts to it.
**Null versus void**: null is a value, `void *` is a type. A `void *` can hold null, a valid address, or anything in between.
**`nullptr`**: C23 adds a typed null pointer constant `nullptr` of type `nullptr_t`, matching C++11.
**Sentinel**: a special value that marks the end of data. Null is the sentinel of pointer-linked structures and of `argv`.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.body:
Take `int *p = NULL;`. The compiler stores the platform's null representation, usually 8 zero bytes, into `p`. `if (p == NULL)` compares those bytes against the null representation. `if (!p)` does the same. Because `p` is null, `*p` would try to access address 0, which the operating system keeps unmapped, so the CPU raises a page fault and the OS delivers `SIGSEGV` to the process. The standard does not promise this; it only says the behavior is undefined, so an optimizer may also assume the pointer is non-null after seeing a dereference and delete a later null check.

The most important usage pattern is to check results that can fail before using them. `malloc` returns null on failure, `fopen` returns null if the file cannot be opened, `strchr` returns null when the character is absent. The program below checks the allocation, treats null as the end of a list, and shows an optional argument.

sections.heading: Variants & Types
bullets: **`NULL` as `((void *)0)`**: the usual C definition. Assignable to any pointer type without a cast.
**Plain `0`**: also a valid null pointer constant in pointer contexts. It is not a null pointer when passed to a variadic function, where it is just an int.
**`nullptr` (C23)**: a keyword for a null pointer constant with its own type. Safe in variadic calls and with `_Generic`.
**Null function pointer**: `void (*cb)(void) = NULL;` marks an optional callback. Check before calling.
**Null-terminated array**: `argv`, `environ` and many option tables end with a `NULL` entry instead of carrying a count.
**Null character vs null pointer**: `'\0'` is a char with value 0 that ends a string. `NULL` is a pointer. `NUL` is the name of the character, `NULL` the pointer.
**Empty string vs null pointer**: `""` is a valid string of length 0. `NULL` is no string at all, and `strlen(NULL)` is undefined.
**Null object pattern**: instead of null, use a real sentinel object (such as a dummy head node) so code needs fewer special cases.

sections.heading: Complexity & Costs
bullets: **Checking for null**: one compare and a branch, effectively free and highly predictable when null is rare.
**Storage**: same as any pointer, 4 or 8 bytes.
**Cost of a missing check**: a crash, or worse, a security hole. The cost of the check is one instruction per use.
**Hoisting checks**: validate once at the function entry or at the API boundary instead of at every use inside a hot loop.
**Optimizer interaction**: after `*p`, the compiler may assume `p != NULL`, so a later `if (p)` may be removed. Place the check before the first use.
**Linked list termination**: a traversal needs n + 1 comparisons for n nodes, and the null test replaces storing a separate length.

**Guard page**: operating systems leave at least the first 4 KB page unmapped, so small offsets from null (`p->field` for a small struct) also trap. Large offsets (index 100000 on a null array pointer) may land in valid memory.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls & Gotchas
bullets: **Dereferencing without checking**: `*malloc(...)` with no test, `fopen` result passed straight to `fgets`. These crash under low memory or a missing file.
**Use after the check fails but code continues**: printing an error and then falling through into the code that dereferences. Use `return`, `exit` or `goto cleanup`.
**`strlen(NULL)`, `printf("%s", NULL)`, `strcmp(NULL, s)`**: undefined. glibc's printf prints `(null)` for a null `%s`, which hides the bug on one platform and crashes on another.
**Confusing `NULL` and `'\0'`**: `if (s[i] == NULL)` compares a char with a pointer, and `*s = NULL` stores a pointer into a char. Both are bugs, the first usually with a warning.
**Freeing and reusing**: `free(p);` leaves `p` dangling, non-null and non-usable. `free(NULL)` is safe, so resetting `p = NULL` after `free` makes double-free harmless.
**Null in variadic calls**: `execl(path, arg0, 0)` passes an int 0, which may be wrong width on 64-bit. Write `(char *)NULL` or `NULL` correctly cast.
**Assuming all-bits-zero**: `memset(&ptr_struct, 0, sizeof ptr_struct)` makes null pointers on mainstream platforms but is not guaranteed by the standard.
**Checking after dereferencing**: `int v = *p; if (!p) return;` lets the compiler remove the check, and the earlier access already invoked undefined behavior.
**Treating null as an error code**: functions that may legitimately return null (like `strchr`) need the caller to distinguish 'not found' from failure.
**Pointer wrapped in a struct**: `if (obj)` does not test `obj->buf`. Check each pointer on the path you dereference.
**Kernel null mappings**: mapping page zero is possible on some systems and has been used in exploits; kernels restrict it with `mmap_min_addr`.

sections.heading: Real-World Use
bullets: **Allocation failure**: `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc` and `strdup` return null on out-of-memory, checked on every call in robust code.
**File and API results**: `fopen`, `getenv`, `fgets` (null at EOF), `strstr`, `bsearch` and `dlsym` signal absence with null.
**Data structures**: next pointers in lists, child pointers in trees, empty buckets in hash tables and the end of a trie path.
**Optional parameters**: `time(NULL)`, `realloc(NULL, n)` equals `malloc(n)`, `waitpid` status pointer, and `sigaction` old-action argument.
**Linux kernel**: `ERR_PTR` and `IS_ERR` encode errors in pointers, with plain null still meaning 'no object'. `BUG_ON(!ptr)` and `WARN_ON` catch violations.
**Safer languages**: Rust uses `Option<&T>` and Java and C# have null reference exceptions, because null mistakes are so common. Tony Hoare called null his billion-dollar mistake.
**Static analysis**: compilers and tools warn with `-Wnonnull`, `__attribute__((nonnull))` and the Clang static analyzer to prove or flag null dereferences.

sections.heading: Interview Notes
bullets: **Q: What is a null pointer?** A pointer value guaranteed not to equal the address of any object or function, produced from a null pointer constant.
**Q: Is NULL always 0?** NULL expands to an implementation-defined null pointer constant. The constant 0 in pointer context is null, but the machine representation need not be all zero bits.
**Q: What happens on dereference?** Undefined behavior. Typically a segmentation fault, because page 0 is unmapped.
**Q: Null versus void pointer?** Null is a value that points nowhere, and any pointer type can hold it. `void *` is a generic type that can hold any address, including null.
**Q: Is `free(NULL)` safe?** Yes, it does nothing. That makes `p = NULL` after `free(p)` a good habit.
**Q: How do you check malloc?** Compare the result with NULL before use, and handle failure by cleaning up and returning an error.
**Q: NULL versus '\0' versus 0?** Pointer, char and int. They hold the same number in many cases but have different types and uses.
**Q: What does `if (p)` mean?** True when `p` is not null.

sections.body: Assign with `= NULL` (or `= 0`), test with `== NULL`, `!= NULL` or just the pointer in a condition. All of these are equivalent. Initialize every pointer you cannot immediately point at an object so that a stray dereference faults predictably rather than corrupting memory.
sections.code:
int *p = NULL;                  // declaration with null
if (p == NULL) puts("empty");   // explicit
if (!p)        puts("empty");   // idiomatic, same meaning
p = &x;                         // now valid
if (p)         printf("%d\n", *p);

subtopics.title: Checking malloc and other results
subtopics.summary: The most common reason to test for null.

sections.body: `malloc(n)` returns null when it cannot allocate. On Linux with overcommit enabled it rarely returns null for ordinary sizes, but the check is still required for portability and for huge sizes. Remember `realloc`: assign to a temporary so a failure does not leak the old block.

subtopics.title: Null pointer dereference
subtopics.summary: What actually happens, and why the compiler may ignore your check.

sections.body: On Linux, the first page of the address space is unmapped, so reading or writing through a null pointer raises a page fault that becomes `SIGSEGV`, producing a core dump. In user programs this is a reliable crash, which is helpful for debugging. In embedded systems address 0 may be real memory, such as a vector table, and a null write silently corrupts it. Since the behavior is undefined, an optimizer that sees `*p` before `if (p == NULL)` may delete the check.

subtopics.title: Null in data structures
subtopics.summary: Terminators for lists, trees and hash chains.

sections.body: A singly linked list ends where `next == NULL`. A tree leaf has two null children. A hash bucket is empty when its head is null. Always initialize new nodes' pointers to NULL so traversals terminate, and watch the empty-structure cases: `head == NULL` is an empty list and must be handled before `head->next`.

subtopics.title: NULL versus void pointer
subtopics.summary: Value versus type, in a short comparison.

bullets: **NULL pointer** is a value meaning 'points to nothing'. Any pointer type may hold it.
**Void pointer** is a type meaning 'address of unspecified object type'. It can hold a real address, or null.
A null pointer of one type compares equal to a null pointer of any other type.
Two void pointers can differ and each can refer to a different object.
`void *p = NULL;` is valid and means a generic pointer that currently points nowhere.

subtopics.title: Safe patterns after free
subtopics.summary: Avoiding dangling pointers and double frees.

sections.body: After releasing memory, set the pointer to null. A second `free(p)` is then harmless and a later dereference crashes immediately instead of corrupting freed memory. A macro or helper that takes the address of the pointer makes this automatic. Note it only fixes the one pointer: other copies of the address still dangle.

bullets: Validate pointer arguments at public API boundaries, return an error code and do not crash the caller.
Use `assert(p != NULL)` for internal contracts that should never be violated. It disappears when `NDEBUG` is defined.
Mark parameters that must not be null with `__attribute__((nonnull))` so the compiler warns about literal null arguments.
Use early return or `goto cleanup` after a failed check so execution never reaches the dereference.
Do not paper over bugs by checking everything. A null that should be impossible deserves an assertion, not silent handling.

subtopics.title: Null pointers in other languages
subtopics.summary: How the same idea is handled elsewhere.

sections.body: C++ used `0` and `NULL` for years and added `nullptr` in C++11 to remove overload ambiguity between `int` and pointer; C23 adopted `nullptr` too. Java and Python raise `NullPointerException` and `AttributeError` on null use. Rust has no null references: absence is `Option<T>`, enforced by the compiler. Understanding C null clarifies why those designs exist.

takeaways: A null pointer is guaranteed to compare unequal to any valid object or function address, and is made by converting the constant 0 or `NULL` to a pointer type.
Dereferencing null is undefined behavior; on mainstream systems it faults with SIGSEGV, but the optimizer may also delete later null checks.
Check the results of `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc`, `fopen`, `strchr` and similar calls before using them.
`free(NULL)` is a safe no-op, so setting a pointer to NULL after free prevents double-free on that pointer.
`NULL` is a pointer, `'\0'` is a character and `0` is an int; do not interchange them.
A null pointer is not the same as an empty string; `strlen(NULL)` and `printf("%s", NULL)` are undefined.
Linked lists, trees and `argv` use NULL as a terminator, so test it before dereferencing the next link.
Check pointers before the first dereference, not after; and use `assert` for impossible cases and error returns for possible ones.
